title: A Cup of Tea, Unpoisoned
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 9 of 40
content:
The Floo network failed while we were halfway back to Hogwarts.

That sentence makes the experience sound almost reasonable.

It was not.

One moment I was spinning through green fire with a case of Snape's journals clutched to my chest. The next, the fireplace threw me out into a pub I had never seen, directly into a basket of umbrellas.

Snape arrived three seconds later with considerably more dignity and considerably less balance.

I caught his elbow.

He caught the mantel.

A woman behind the bar looked up from polishing a glass.

“Network's down north of Birmingham,” she said. “Storm charms. Could be an hour.”

Snape closed his eyes.

I pulled an umbrella out from under my knee.

“Well,” I said. “At least we aren't dead.”

He opened one eye.

“You have set an alarmingly low standard for travel.”

“It has served me well.”

The pub was called The Copper Kettle. It occupied the back half of what looked from the street like a closed tailor's shop. There were six tables, a crooked bar, and a fire that smelled of cedar.

We took the table furthest from everyone else.

Naturally.

The woman brought tea without asking.

Snape looked at the cup.

Then at her.

“I remember you,” she said.

His face went blank.

“You came through here in ninety-four. Bought a vial of salamander blood from my brother and told him his preservation charm was embarrassing.”

“It was.”

“He fixed it.”

“Then the humiliation was educational.”

She laughed and walked away.

I stared at him.

“What?”

“You leave a trail of improved storage charms and emotional damage everywhere you go.”

“A legacy requires consistency.”

The tea was ordinary black tea, strong enough to be useful.

I added milk.

Snape did not.

I pointed at his cup. “Are you going to test it?”

His eyebrow lifted.

“For poison,” I said.

“I understood the question.”

“Given your life, it seems reasonable.”

He picked up the cup and drank.

“No?”

“If someone wished to poison me in a provincial pub, they would deserve the success.”

“That is not a healthy attitude.”

“It is an efficient one.”

I sighed.

He looked faintly satisfied.

Outside, rain streaked the windows. The delay gave us nowhere to go and nothing useful to do. I could have read one of the journals, but that felt intrusive while he sat across from me.

So I watched the storm.

Snape watched me.

“You dislike idle time,” he said.

“So do you.”

“I asked first.”

“No, you made an observation.”

His mouth tightened.

“Yes,” I said. “I dislike it.”

“Why?”

That surprised me.

He almost never asked questions that were not tactical.

I considered giving him something easy.

Instead I said, “If I'm doing something, I know what I'm for.”

The words sounded too honest once they existed.

Snape looked at his tea.

“Utility is not identity.”

I laughed once.

“That's rich coming from you.”

His eyes lifted.

“Explain.”

“You spent years making yourself useful to people who could not know what you were doing. Dumbledore needed a spy. Voldemort needed a servant. Hogwarts needed a teacher. Slytherin needed a Head of House. Harry needed someone keeping him alive from the shadows.”

I stopped.

Snape's face had gone very still.

“I've read the public testimony,” I added. “Not your memories.”

“I know.”

“And now you're recovering by turning yourself into an evidence archive with legs.”

His lip curled.

“Poetic.”

“Accurate.”

“Presumptuous.”

“Also accurate.”

The woman behind the bar dropped a spoon. The clatter filled the pause.

At last Snape said, “And what are you when you are not useful?”

The question found a place I had not armored.

I looked out the window.

“Annoying, apparently.”

“That is a skill, not an identity.”

I smiled despite myself.

“I'm still figuring it out.”

He nodded once.

No advice.

No lecture.

No attempt to fix me.

I appreciated it more than reassurance.

The storm worsened.

Someone near the bar started a card game. A wireless crackled with a news report about reconstruction grants and Ministry hearings. Snape's shoulders tightened when his name was mentioned.

The announcer called him “the controversial former Headmaster.”

I reached over and turned the wireless down.

Snape looked at my hand.

“I am capable of hearing criticism.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I was trying to drink tea, and the man's voice is irritating.”

A pause.

“Accurate,” Snape said.

I smiled.

The woman brought sandwiches.

“We didn't order these,” I said.

“House rule during network outages.”

Snape eyed the plate.

“Unpoisoned?” I asked.

He gave me a look.

I took the first bite.

“Heroic,” he said.

“Someone has to protect you.”

His expression changed so quickly I almost missed it.

The joke had hit something real.

I put the sandwich down.

“I didn't mean—”

“I know.”

His voice was quiet.

That should have ended it.

Instead he said, “People have protected me.”

I waited.

“Few did so without expecting a return.”

“Dumbledore?”

He looked at me sharply.

“You said few. Not none.”

His gaze dropped.

“Albus expected a great deal.”

“That doesn't answer the question.”

“No.”

I waited again.

He seemed annoyed by my refusal to fill the silence.

At last he said, “He kept me alive when I gave him little reason to.”

“And then used you.”

“Yes.”

“Both can be true.”

His eyes met mine.

“Yes.”

It was one of the quietest agreements we had ever reached.

I picked up my sandwich.

After a moment, he picked up his.

We ate.

The network remained down for another ninety minutes.

During that time, I learned that Snape hated sweet tea, preferred coffee but considered most public coffee an offense, could play chess but found competitive chess players tedious, and had once brewed a hangover cure for Professor McGonagall after a staff Christmas party.

He denied the last detail as soon as he realized he had told me enough to make it funny.

“You are not repeating that.”

“To anyone?”

“To anyone.”

“Can I repeat it to you?”

“No.”

“What if I write it down?”

His stare promised consequences.

I laughed.

He looked at me over the rim of his cup.

There was something strange in his face.

Not warmth exactly.

Attention.

The kind that made me suddenly aware of the shape of my hands around the teacup and the rain cooling the window beside us.

My pulse changed.

Snape's eyes narrowed.

Of course he noticed.

He noticed everything.

I looked away first.

That was new.

The Floo flared green.

“Northbound connections restored,” the bartender called.

We stood.

Snape lifted the lighter case.

I took the heavier one.

He did not argue.

At the hearth, he paused.

“The tea was poor,” he said.

“It was fine.”

“It was tannic.”

“So are you.”

He stared at me.

Then the corner of his mouth lifted.

“After you.”

I stepped into the green fire.

As the world began to spin, I realized I had just spent two hours trapped in a pub with Severus Snape and had not once wished for the network to return sooner.

That was probably a problem.

The delay gave us time to read three of the journals properly. Two were worthless inventories. The third contained a set of notes from a St Mungo's brewer who had studied long-term nerve damage after venom exposure.

Snape read the same paragraph four times.

“You've found something,” I said.

“No.”

“You've been glaring at that page like it owes you money.”

He slid the journal across the table.

The treatment was experimental, old, and probably useless. It was also the first reference either of us had found to a tremor pattern that resembled his.

“Worth asking Pomfrey?”

“Possibly.”

“That's practically enthusiasm.”

His finger tapped the margin. “It is a twenty-seven-year-old case series with six patients.”

“So: not magic.”

“Despite the setting, evidence remains advisable.”

I smiled. “I'll copy the citation.”

He looked at me oddly.

“What?”

“You did not say it would work.”

“No.”

“Most people do.”

I understood then. Hope had become another thing people tried to force on him, as if optimism were a debt he owed for surviving.

“It might help,” I said. “That's enough to investigate.”

His gaze lowered to the journal.

“Yes,” he said. “It is.”

I carried it back to Hogwarts with the journals.

ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors

let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception

dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent

attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
